trace.title: Step-by-step trace
trace.caption: Each step that changed a variable
trace.more_one: … {{count}} more step follows the same pattern.
trace.more_other: … {{count}} more steps follow the same pattern.

variableTracking.name: Variable Tracking
variableTracking.tagline: Keep every variable straight, line by line.
variableTracking.description: A short program updates several variables with assignments, copies and swaps. Follow it line by line and say what a variable holds at the end, at a given line, or which one ends up largest.
variableTracking.scoringSummary: Each question has one exact answer, computed by running the program. Your result is the share answered correctly, with a small bonus for pace; nothing is timed out.

instructions.order: The program runs from top to bottom, one line at a time.
instructions.copy: “x = y” copies the value y has right now; changing y later does not change x.
instructions.swap: A swap uses a helper: temp = a, a = b, b = temp.
instructions.typed: From level 4 you type the exact number. After answering, the full trace is shown.

variableTracking.simpleInstructions: Read the lines one by one and keep track of each box’s number.

levels.1: Two variables, two updates: follow each assignment in order.
levels.3: Copies keep the value they were given: later changes do not follow them.
levels.4: Swaps through a helper variable; type the exact value.
levels.5: Stop in the middle: the value right after a given line.
levels.6: Four variables and updates that combine several of them.
levels.7: Longer programs: six updates over four variables.
levels.8: Seven updates; most of them read the variable they overwrite.
levels.9: Five variables, chained swaps and nested expressions.
levels.10: Everything at once: eight updates over five variables.

prompt.finalValue: What is the value of {{name}} when the program ends?
prompt.afterLine: What is the value of {{name}} right after line {{line}} runs?
prompt.largest: Which of {{names}} holds the largest value when the program ends?

explanation.finalValue: Step by step — {{steps}}. So {{name}} ends at {{value}}.
explanation.afterLine: Up to line {{line}} — {{steps}}. So {{name}} is {{value}} at that point (it ends at {{final}}).
explanation.largest: Step by step — {{steps}}. At the end {{final}}, so {{winner}} is the largest.

conditionalLogic.name: Conditional Logic
conditionalLogic.description: Read if / elif / else chains with and, or and not, and decide what a program prints for given inputs — or which input leads to a given output. Later levels nest conditions and test short-circuit evaluation.
conditionalLogic.scoringSummary: Every answer is checked by running the program with the interpreter. Your result is the share answered correctly, with a small bonus for pace; answering is not timed.

instructions.order: Conditions are checked from the top: the first true one runs its block, the rest are skipped.
instructions.operators: “and” needs both sides true; “or” needs at least one; “not” flips true and false.
instructions.backwards: Some questions give you an output and ask which input produces it.
instructions.shortCircuit: From level 8: “and” stops at the first false side and “or” at the first true one — a division the program never reaches cannot fail.

conditionalLogic.simpleInstructions: Check each condition from the top; the first true one decides what is printed.

levels.1: One input, one comparison per branch: the first true condition wins.
levels.5: Ifs inside ifs: only one inner chain ever runs.
levels.6: Work backwards: which input produces this output?
levels.7: Five outcomes and conditions that mix “and” with “or”.
levels.8: Short-circuit: “and” stops at the first false, “or” at the first true.
levels.9: Guards in the wrong order: spot the condition that crashes.
levels.10: Everything at once: nested chains, mixed logic and short-circuits.

conditionalLogic.errorOutcome: Stops with an error (division by zero)

prompt.happens: What happens when this program runs?
prompt.letter: Which letter does this program print?
prompt.findInput: Which input makes this program print {{target}}?

explanation.stepError: line {{line}}: “{{cond}}” evaluates the division first, with y = 0 → error
explanation.runError: With {{inputs}}: {{steps}} — so the program stops with an error. “and” / “or” only skip the right side when the left side already decides the result.

view.label: Program with conditions
view.fromOptions: The inputs come from the options. Which one makes it print {{target}}?
view.inputsDivision_one: Lines 1–{{count}} set the inputs. Dividing by zero stops the program with an error.
view.inputsDivision_other: Lines 1–{{count}} set the inputs. Dividing by zero stops the program with an error.

algorithmicLogic.name: Algorithm Tracing
algorithmicLogic.description: Order tasks that depend on each other, trace language-neutral pseudocode and solve deployment puzzles. Trains deduction, conditional reasoning and algorithmic thinking.
algorithmicLogic.scoringSummary: Points for each correct answer, scaled by level, with a bonus for pace and streaks; a wrong answer costs a quarter of the base. Accuracy is 75% of the performance index.

instructions.read: Read the whole challenge before answering: every rule, arrow and line matters.
instructions.arrow: An arrow “x → y” means x must finish before y starts.
instructions.pseudocode: Pseudocode runs top to bottom; “set a ← b + 1” stores the new value in a.
instructions.exact: From level 4 some answers are exact numbers — work them out, there are no options to guess from.

levels.1: Follow simple dependencies and straight-line assignments.
levels.2: Branching: evaluate a condition and follow only the branch it selects.
levels.3: Near-miss orders and your first constraint puzzles: verify every rule.
levels.4: Compound conditions and exact answers: no options to lean on.
levels.5: Loops and transitive dependencies: reason about what happens repeatedly and indirectly.
levels.6: Conditions inside loops: state changes the path on every iteration.
levels.7: Open-ended loops and deduction chains across six services.
levels.8: Parallel scheduling: find the chain that bounds the whole build.
levels.9: Weighted schedules, nested loops and seven-service deductions with weak clues.
levels.10: Everything at once: large weighted graphs, long traces and only relative clues.

rules.notAdjacent: {{a}} and {{b}} are not deployed next to each other

prompt.arrangement: Services are deployed one per slot, left to right. Which deployment order satisfies every rule?
prompt.position: Services are deployed one per slot, left to right. Which service is deployed in slot {{slot}}?

explanation.arrangement: The only arrangement that satisfies every rule is {{arrangement}}. {{reasons}}.
explanation.position: The only arrangement that satisfies every rule is {{arrangement}}. So slot {{slot}} holds {{answer}}.

dependencyOrder.prompt: Each arrow means the left module must run before the right one. Which execution order is valid?
dependencyOrder.explanation: {{order}} runs every module after all of its dependencies (other valid orders may exist, but none of them was offered). {{reasons}}.

dependencyCount.prompt: How many modules must finish (directly or indirectly) before {{target}} can start?

prompt.weighted: Independent modules can run in parallel. What is the minimum number of rounds (each module takes the rounds shown) to finish everything?
prompt.unweighted: Independent modules can run in parallel. What is the minimum number of rounds (each module takes one round) to finish everything?

criticalPath.explanation_one: The longest dependency chain is {{path}}, which takes {{count}} round; everything else fits in parallel alongside it.
criticalPath.explanation_other: The longest dependency chain is {{path}}, which takes {{count}} rounds; everything else fits in parallel alongside it.

programTrace.prompt: What is the value of {{name}} after the program runs?
programTrace.explanation: Tracing the program line by line ends with {{state}}, so {{result}}.

view.arrowMeaning: x → y means x runs before y

loopPrediction.name: Loop Prediction
loopPrediction.tagline: How many turns, and what is left at the end?
loopPrediction.description: Predict what for and while loops do: how many times a line runs, what an accumulator holds at the end, or the last value printed. Later levels nest loops and exit early.
loopPrediction.scoringSummary: Every answer comes from running the program with the interpreter. Your result is the share answered correctly, with a small bonus for pace; answering is not timed.

instructions.range: “for i in range(a, b)” runs with i = a, a + 1, … up to b − 1 (b itself is not included).
instructions.while: “while” checks its condition before every turn and stops as soon as it is false.
instructions.nested: An inner loop starts again from the beginning on every turn of the outer loop.
instructions.return: “return” inside a loop ends the whole function at once. After answering, the trace is shown.

loopPrediction.simpleInstructions: Count the turns of the loop and keep track of the numbers as they change.

levels.1: Count the turns of a simple loop and add up as it goes.
levels.2: While loops: the condition is checked before every turn.
levels.3: An if inside the loop: not every turn changes the total.
levels.5: A loop inside a loop: the inner one restarts every outer turn.
levels.6: Early exits: a return inside a loop ends it at once.
levels.8: Inner loops whose length depends on the outer variable.
levels.9: Stop conditions joined with “and”: which one ends the loop first?
levels.10: Everything at once, with up to nine turns per loop.

prompt.iterations: How many times does line {{line}} run?
prompt.finalValue: What is the value of {{name}} when the program ends?
prompt.lastOutput: What is the last value this program prints?

explanation.iterations_one: Line {{line}} ran {{count}} time. Step by step — {{steps}}.
explanation.iterations_other: Line {{line}} ran {{count}} times. Step by step — {{steps}}.
explanation.lastOutput_one: It prints {{shown}} — {{count}} value, the last is {{last}}. Step by step — {{steps}}.
explanation.lastOutput_other: It prints {{shown}} — {{count}} values, the last is {{last}}. Step by step — {{steps}}.

view.label: Program with loops
view.count: Count every time line {{line}} (highlighted) runs, across all turns.
view.followVariable: Follow the variable through every turn.
view.output: Each print adds one value to the output.

codeScan.name: Code Comparison
codeScan.tagline: Spot the one token that changed.
codeScan.description: Compare an original pseudocode snippet with its copy and spot the single changed token — an operator, a swapped variable, an off-by-one number, a misspelled name or a negated condition. Trains processing speed, rapid comparison and fast error detection.
codeScan.scoringSummary: Speed is the trained ability: the pace bonus is doubled and pace is 40% of the performance index, but a wrong answer costs points.

instructions.layout: The original is on the left (or on top), the copy on the right (or below).
instructions.oneToken: When the snippets differ, exactly one token of one line changed; everything else is identical.
instructions.point: To point at a changed line, click it (or focus it with Tab and press Enter) in the copy.
instructions.kinds: Change kinds: operator (< → <=, + → -, and → or), variable swapped for another one in the snippet, number changed, name misspelled, or “not” added to a condition.
instructions.speed: Speed counts more than in other games — but a wrong answer costs points, so stay precise.

levels.1: Compare two short snippets and decide whether they are identical.
levels.2: Point at the exact line that changed; misspelled names join the mix.
levels.3: Negated conditions and one-character changes: read every token, not the shape.
levels.4: Nested blocks and compound conditions: more places for a change to hide.
levels.5: Runs of look-alike lines: compare token by token, not line shape.
levels.6: Longer listings under a tighter clock; most changes are one character.
levels.7: Name the kind of change: operator, variable, number, typo or negation.
levels.8: Classify fine changes hidden among look-alike lines, faster.
levels.9: Find and classify the change with no hint: locate first, then name it.
levels.10: Twelve dense, near-identical lines and a one-character change: at full speed.

prompt.sameOrDifferent: Is the copy identical to the original?
prompt.findTheChange: One token of the copy differs from the original. Which line of the copy changed?
prompt.classify: One token of the copy changed. What kind of change is it?
prompt.classifyLine: Line {{line}} of the copy has one changed token. What kind of change is it?

change.variable: On line {{line}}, the variable “{{before}}” was replaced by “{{after}}”, another variable of the snippet: “{{from}}” → “{{to}}”.
change.typo: On line {{line}}, the name “{{before}}” was misspelled as “{{after}}”: “{{from}}” → “{{to}}”.
change.negation: On line {{line}}, “not” was added in front of the condition, negating it: “{{from}}” → “{{to}}”.

explanation.same_one: {{label}}: all {{count}} lines match token for token.
explanation.same_other: {{label}}: all {{count}} lines match token for token.

view.identical: No line differs: the snippets are identical.

dependencyOrdering.name: Dependency Ordering
dependencyOrdering.tagline: What has to happen before what?
dependencyOrdering.description: Build steps, kitchen prep and release tasks, each with the tasks it needs. Find what can start, what is unblocked, a complete valid order — and which new need would create a cycle.
dependencyOrdering.scoringSummary: Each question has exactly one right answer, checked by a graph solver. Your result is the share answered correctly, with a small bonus for pace; answering is not timed.

instructions.needs: “A needs B” means B must be finished before A can start.
instructions.listed: Only the listed needs count — not what you would do in a real kitchen or project.
instructions.arrows: To order tasks, use the arrow buttons next to each one, then submit.
instructions.cycle: A cycle (A needs B, B needs A, possibly through other tasks) makes every order impossible.

dependencyOrdering.simpleInstructions: Do each task only after the tasks it needs are done.

levels.1: Find the task that needs nothing.
levels.2: Chain every task into the only order that works.
levels.3: Some work is done: what is unblocked now?
levels.4: Several orders could work: pick the one option that does.
levels.5: Near misses: each wrong order breaks a single need.
levels.6: Cycles: which new need would make every order impossible?
levels.7: Hidden cycles: the loop runs through other tasks.
levels.9: Nine tasks: long chains and long hidden cycles.
levels.10: Everything at once on ten tasks.

prompt.readyNext: The ticked tasks are done. Which of these can start now?
prompt.fullOrder: There is only one order that respects every need. Put the tasks in that order.
prompt.cycle: Which new need would create a cycle, so that no order could ever work?

explanation.startFirst: {{task}} is the only task that needs nothing. The others must wait: {{others}}.
explanation.readyNextFree: {{needs}}, and so it was free to start. The others still wait: {{others}}.
explanation.readyNextDone: {{needs}}, and all of that is done. The others still wait: {{others}}.
explanation.fullOrder: {{first}} needs nothing, then each task needs the one before it: {{steps}}.
explanation.fullOrderExtra: {{first}} needs nothing, then each task needs the one before it: {{steps}}. The extra needs ({{extra}}) are already satisfied by that chain.
explanation.validOrder: Only {{order}} keeps every task after what it needs: {{others}}.
explanation.brokenOrder: the order with {{task}} before {{prerequisite}} fails because {{task}} needs {{prerequisite}}
explanation.cycle: {{loop}} already runs in that order (each one before the next). If {{task}} also needed {{prerequisite}}, it would have to come before itself. The other new needs keep at least one valid order.

view.tasks: Tasks and what each one needs
view.cycleHint: Each option adds one new need to the list above. Exactly one of them closes a loop.

algorithmConstruction.name: Algorithm Construction
algorithmConstruction.tagline: Put the blocks in the order that works.
algorithmConstruction.description: You get the pieces of a program and the output it must print. Arrange the blocks so it prints exactly that; later levels add loops and a spare block that is not needed.
algorithmConstruction.scoringSummary: An order counts as correct only when it is the single order that prints the target; every possible order is checked with the interpreter when the challenge is made. Untimed, with a small bonus for pace.

instructions.target: The program must print exactly the output shown above the blocks.
instructions.variables: A line can only use a variable that an earlier block has already set.
instructions.move: Move blocks with the ↑ / ↓ buttons, then submit. Loop blocks move as a whole.
instructions.spare: From level 6 one block is a spare: the program does not use it — move it to the end.

algorithmConstruction.simpleInstructions: Put the code blocks in the order that prints the number shown.

levels.1: Three blocks: set a value, change it, print it.
levels.2: Four blocks: each line needs a value set by an earlier one.
levels.3: Three variables: find which block can only come after which.
levels.4: A loop block: what happens before the loop changes what it produces.
levels.6: A spare block: one block is not needed — put it last.
levels.9: Two loops and a spare block.
levels.10: Always a spare: two loops, three variables, one block too many.

prompt.orderBlocks: Order the blocks so the program prints {{printed}}.
prompt.spareBlock: Order the blocks so the program prints {{printed}}. One block is not needed: put it last.

explanation.orderBlocks_one: Only {{order}} prints {{printed}} (the only possible order was checked with the interpreter). Step by step — {{steps}}.
explanation.orderBlocks_other: Only {{order}} prints {{printed}} (all {{count}} possible orders were checked with the interpreter; the others print something else or stop with an error). Step by step — {{steps}}.
explanation.spareBlock_one: Only {{order}} prints {{printed}} (the only possible order was checked with the interpreter). Block {{spare}} is the spare: no order that uses it prints {{printed}}. Step by step — {{steps}}.
explanation.spareBlock_other: Only {{order}} prints {{printed}} (all {{count}} possible orders were checked with the interpreter; the others print something else or stop with an error). Block {{spare}} is the spare: no order that uses it prints {{printed}}. Step by step — {{steps}}.

view.spare: One block is not needed: it goes last.

bugHunter.name: Bug Hunter
bugHunter.tagline: One artifact, a few rules, exactly one bug.
bugHunter.description: Scan logs, data records and pseudocode against explicit rules and point at the single item that breaks one. Trains selective and sustained attention, anomaly detection and debugging.
bugHunter.scoringSummary: Points for each anomaly found, scaled by level, with pace and streak bonuses. Accuracy is 75% of the performance index.

instructions.rules: Read the rules first: only the stated rules count, not what “looks” wrong.
instructions.check: Then check the items one by one. Exactly one item breaks exactly one rule.
instructions.above: Rules about “the item above” compare each item only with its direct neighbour.
instructions.nearMisses: Many items are near-misses — unusual but legal. Click (or press Enter on) the bug to answer.

levels.1: Hold one rule in mind and check a short list against it, item by item.
levels.2: Read pseudocode as data: find the line that breaks a naming or ordering rule.
levels.3: Subtle bugs: typos, off-by-one values and seconds out of order.
levels.4: Two rules at once, and resources that must be opened and closed correctly.
levels.5: Mixed rule families: compare with the line above and check each field.
levels.6: Longer artifacts with more decoys: stay accurate all the way down.
levels.7: Three rules per item, including conditions that only apply to some items.
levels.8: Dense artifacts where most suspicious-looking items are legal.
levels.9: Sustained attention: three rules over three dozen noisy items.
levels.10: Everything at once: 42 items, three rules, heavy noise and near-misses everywhere.

prompt.sequenceAnomaly: Scan the log. Exactly one line breaks a rule — which one?
prompt.schemaViolation: Validate the records against the schema. Exactly one record is invalid — which one?
prompt.multiRule: Every log line must satisfy all the rules. Exactly one line breaks one of them — which one?
prompt.codeRule: Review the program. Exactly one line breaks a rule — which one?

rule.consecutive: Each {{field}} is exactly 1 more than the {{field}} on the item above.
rule.ascendingTime: Each {{field}} is the same as or later than the {{field}} on the item above.
rule.unique: No {{field}} repeats a {{field}} used on an earlier item.
rule.range: {{field}} is a whole number from {{min}} to {{max}}.
rule.digits_one: {{field}} is a whole number with exactly {{count}} digit.
rule.digits_other: {{field}} is a whole number with exactly {{count}} digits.
rule.email: {{field}} has exactly one "@", a name before it and a dotted domain after it (name@domain.tld).
rule.semver: {{field}} is three whole numbers separated by dots (major.minor.patch).
rule.impliesRange: When {{when}} is {{equals}}, {{field}} is a whole number from {{min}} to {{max}}.
rule.definedBeforeUse: Every variable is assigned with “set” on an earlier line before it is read.
rule.closeOpened: Every “open x” is followed by a “close x” on a later line.
rule.writeWhileOpen: “write … to x” only happens while x is open (after “open x”, before “close x”).
rule.camelCase: Every name is camelCase: it starts with a lower-case letter and uses only letters and digits (no “_”).

emailProblem.badDomain: has "{{domain}}" after the "@", which is not a dotted domain

reason.invalidTime: {{field}}={{value}} is not a valid HH:MM:SS time
reason.earlier: {{field}}={{value}} is earlier than {{previous}} on the item above

unassigned.here: it reads {{name}}, which has not been assigned yet (this line is the first to set it)
unassigned.later: it reads {{name}}, which has not been assigned yet (it is first set on line {{line}})

reason.neverClosed: {{resource}} is opened here but never closed afterwards

write.openedLater: it writes to {{resource}}, which is only opened later, on line {{line}}
write.neverOpened: it writes to {{resource}}, which is never opened

explanation.numbered: Item {{item}} is the bug: {{reason}}. It breaks rule {{number}}: {{rule}}
explanation.single: Item {{item}} is the bug: {{reason}}. It breaks the rule: {{rule}}

view.rules: Rules — every item must satisfy all of them

codeMemory.name: Code Memory
codeMemory.tagline: Records, calls, state and positions — from memory.
codeMemory.description: Study records, API call sequences, variable assignments and keyword grids, then answer once they are hidden. Trains the working, sequential and contextual memory you use when you keep a data structure or a trace in your head.
codeMemory.scoringSummary: Points for each correct recall, scaled by level, with small pace and streak bonuses. Accuracy is 75% of the performance index.

instructions.study: Every challenge starts with a study phase: memorise what you see, then press “I’m ready” or wait for the timer.
instructions.hidden: The material is hidden before the question appears, so you will not know in advance what is asked.
instructions.assignments: Assignments run top to bottom; “y = x + 2” stores the new value in y.
instructions.exact: From level 4 some answers are exact numbers, and from level 5 you may have to rebuild a whole call order.

levels.1: Hold a few fields, calls and positions in mind for a few seconds.
levels.2: Keep two records apart and track a variable through an update.
levels.3: Remember what followed what, and positions on a larger grid.
levels.4: Exact answers: compute and hold three variables with no options to lean on.
levels.5: Interference: look-alike ids and keywords, and rebuilding a full call order.
levels.6: Similar calls on the same resources: encode the exact order, not the gist.
levels.7: Look records up by another field and recall state at a given line.
levels.8: Four records, four variables and eight similar calls held at once.
levels.9: Joins: follow a foreign key between two tables you can no longer see.
levels.10: Maximum load and interference with the shortest study time per item.

record.prompt: What was the {{field}} of the {{type}} record?
record.explanation: The {{type}} record was {{record}}, so its {{field}} was {{value}}.

crossReference.prompt: The {{type}} whose {{key}} was {{keyValue}} — what was its {{field}}?

join.explanation: The {{parent}} with {{key}} {{keyValue}} had id {{parentId}}; the {{child}} with {{link}} was {{record}}, so its {{field}} was {{value}}.

prompt.order: Put the calls back in the order they ran.

explanation.order: The calls ran in this order: {{calls}}.
explanation.successor: The sequence was {{calls}}; right after {{call}} came {{answer}}.

prompt.final: What was the final value of {{name}}?
prompt.afterLine: What was the value of {{name}} right after line {{line}}?

explanation.afterLine: {{steps}}; so right after line {{line}}, {{name}} was {{value}} (it later became {{later}}).

position.explanationTwin: {{keyword}} was in {{cell}}. The look-alike {{twin}} was in {{twinCell}}.

view.callsHeading: Calls, in the order they ran

patternArchitect.name: Pattern Architect
patternArchitect.tagline: Find the rule, then apply it.
patternArchitect.description: Continue number sequences, complete symbol grids, infer hidden programs from examples and recognise the same structure under different names. Trains pattern recognition, abstraction and generalisation.
patternArchitect.scoringSummary: Points for each rule found and applied, scaled by level, with pace and streak bonuses. Accuracy is 75% of the performance index.

instructions.rule: Every challenge hides one rule. Find a rule that explains everything shown, then apply it.
instructions.grids: Grids: shapes and counts can follow different rules — check rows and columns separately.
instructions.programs: Hidden programs chain a few simple steps from the listed vocabulary; the order of the steps matters.
instructions.trees: Trees are written as a(b, c): a contains b and c, in that order. Graphs match when renaming the nodes makes every arrow line up.

levels.1: Spot a single regularity: a constant step, or one attribute changing in a grid.
levels.2: Steps that change and grids where two attributes follow separate rules.
levels.3: Two sequences woven together, and grids whose counts follow arithmetic.
levels.4: Infer a hidden one-step program from input → output examples.
levels.5: Programs of two chained steps: separate what each step contributes.
levels.6: Data-dependent steps (repeats, pairs, running totals) with fewer examples.
levels.7: Structure over content: match graphs by shape and restructure trees by analogy.
levels.8: Three-step programs, bigger graphs and tree rules from a single example.
levels.9: Look-alike structures with identical arrow counts, and two-step tree rules.
levels.10: Minimal evidence: three-step programs, seven-node look-alikes, composed tree rules.

sequence.explanationTrap: Rule: {{rule}}. So after {{last}} comes {{answer}}. Repeating only the last step would give {{repeated}}.

sequenceRule.growingStep: the step grows by {{n}} every time ({{steps}}, …)
sequenceRule.shrinkingStep: the step shrinks by {{n}} every time ({{steps}}, …)
sequenceRule.interleaved: two sequences take turns: the 1st, 3rd, 5th… terms go {{odd}}, the 2nd, 4th, 6th… terms go {{even}}
sequenceRule.stepCycle: the steps repeat in a cycle of three: {{steps}}
sequenceRule.sumOfPreviousTwo: each term is the sum of the two before it

grid.explanation: Shapes: {{shapes}}. Counts: {{counts}}. So the missing cell ({{position}}) is {{cell}} — {{description}}.

layer.shiftRight: each row is the row above moved one place to the right (the last wraps to the front)

layer.rowDown: along each row (left to right) the count goes down by one
layer.columnUp: along each column (top to bottom) the count goes up by one
layer.columnDown: along each column (top to bottom) the count goes down by one
layer.rowSum: in each row the last count is the sum of the others
layer.columnSum: in each column the bottom count is the sum of the others

listOp.rotateRight: move the last item to the front
listOp.removeRepeats: remove repeated values (keep the first of each)
listOp.runningTotal: replace each item by the total so far

vocabulary.rotate: move the first item to the end, or the last item to the front
vocabulary.drop: remove the first item, or the last item
vocabulary.keepParity: keep only the even numbers, or only the odd numbers
vocabulary.takeFirst: keep only the first 2 or 3 items
vocabulary.removeRepeats: remove repeated values (keep the first of each)
vocabulary.runningTotal: replace each item by the total so far

transform.prompt: The same hidden program turns every input into its output. What does it produce for the new input?
transform.explanation_one: The hidden program: {{steps}}. Applied to the new input: {{path}}, so the answer is {{answer}}. Every program of up to {{count}} step that fits all the examples gives this same result.
transform.explanation_other: The hidden program: {{steps}}. Applied to the new input: {{path}}, so the answer is {{answer}}. Every program of up to {{count}} steps that fits all the examples gives this same result.

treeOp.mirrorTop: reverse only the order of the top-level items
treeOp.rotateTop: move the first top-level item to the end
treeOp.pruneLeaves: remove every item that has no children
treeOp.flatten: flatten: every item becomes a direct child of the root, in reading order
